title: Gurmukh and manmukh
hookLine: the one facing the Guru and the one facing only their own mind

cards: Young sunflowers do something lovely. In the morning their heads turn east, toward the light, and by evening they've followed it west. Now suppose one sunflower decided to face a mirror instead.
It would see a very handsome sunflower. It would also, slowly, stop growing. Where you face shapes what you become.
The Guru Granth Sahib has two words for the two ways a person can face, and they appear on page after page. Today's word is the first of them: gurmukh.

teach.b: Gurmukh is two words joined: gur, the Guru, and mukh, the face, or the mouth. A gurmukh is someone whose face is turned toward the Guru. Its opposite is manmukh.

teach.h: MAN + MUKH — FACING YOUR OWN MIND.
teach.b: Man is the mind, the restless self; a manmukh faces only their own mind, their own wants, their own reflection.
Sikh teachers often read these less as two tribes of people, good ones and bad ones, than as two directions, and a person can turn either way in a single afternoon. The hymns paint them clearly.
The manmukh is busy and anxious, driven by the five thieves we met a few days ago, always chasing the next thing, like someone wandering in the dark. The gurmukh has no special title.
It's someone who listens to the Guru's word, remembers the Name, works honestly and serves, and so finds a kind of steadiness.

teach.h: THE GURU IS NOW THE WORD.
teach.b: Guru Nanak's great conversation with the yogis, the Sidh Gosht, keeps coming back to this word: it is through the Guru, facing the Guru, that one comes to understand.

And for Sikhs, the Guru is now the Guru Granth Sahib, the Word itself. So facing the Guru can be as simple as opening the book, listening to a hymn, or letting a line of it question you before you act. The test is small.
Before I do this, which way am I facing: toward what I'd do if I were listening to the Guru, or toward the mirror?

how: Sikhs use gurmukh for a person oriented toward the Guru's teaching and manmukh for one led by their own mind; many turn to the Guru Granth Sahib, through daily reading or kirtan, as the way of facing the Guru.

o: a holy man given a special title by the Sikhs
one turned toward the Guru's word, not the mind
the script the Sikh scriptures are written in

games.q: what's inside the two words — tap the pairs.

s: gurmukh and manmukh are two fixed kinds of people
teachers read them as two directions; a person can turn either way.
gurmukh: the one whose face is turned toward the Guru.
the Sidh Gosht keeps returning to the word gurmukh
Guru Nanak's conversation with the yogis says understanding comes through facing the Guru.

games.q: the Guru is now the Guru Granth Sahib. how might someone face the Guru on an ordinary day?
o: only by traveling to a special city.
by listening to a hymn or letting a line of the Word question them before they act.
games.why: facing the Guru can be as simple as opening the book or hearing a hymn, and letting it turn you.

practice: Think of one choice waiting for you, a message, a task, a conversation, and picture yourself turned toward the mirror, choosing only for your own comfort.

Now turn, the way a sunflower turns, toward the best you know: truth, kindness, the Guru's word if that's your path. See how the choice looks from there, settle on one good turn, and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Gurmukh. The one whose face is turned toward the Guru. Its opposite, manmukh, faces only its own mind. Anyone can turn either way.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: gurmukh, the one facing the Guru; the script itself is called Gurmukhi, 'from the Guru's mouth'.

carryVoice: Your line: face the guru. Where you face, you grow. Day two hundred forty-two, done.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 938–946 (Sidh Gosht, Ramkali Mahala 1)
Guru Granth Sahib, gurmukh and manmukh contrasted throughout (e.g. Sri Rag and Maru hymns of Guru Amar Das)
